The fundamental trade-off in every investment decision is between current consumption and future wealth creation. An investor sacrifices liquidity and certainty today in the hope of earning a return that compensates for: The time value of money (waiting) Expected inflation (purchasing power risk) Risk of default or capital loss (uncertainty) Formally, investment may be defined as: “The sacrifice of certain present value for the uncertain future value” — Sharpe, Alexander & Bailey (2020) In the Indian regulatory context, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) defines investment as the purchase of financial assets with the expectation of income or capital appreciation over time. 1.1.2 Investment vs. Speculation vs. Gambling Dimension Investment Speculation Gambling Time Horizon Long-term (1+ years) Short-term (days–months) Immediate Risk Level Moderate High Extremely High Basis of Decision Fundamental analysis, research Market trends, tips, momentum Chance, luck Expected Return Reasonable, commensurate with risk High, risk-adjusted Unpredictable Leverage Used Rarely Often Always Regulatory Framework SEBI, AMFI, RBI SEBI (F&O segment) Unregulated / illegal Capital Protection Primary objective Secondary concern No concern Source: Compiled based on SEBI guidelines and standard finance literature. 1.1.3 Characteristics of Investment Every sound investment exhibits the following essential characteristics: 1. Return: All investments are made with the expectation of earning a return. Return may take the form of: - Dividend (equity shares) - Interest (bonds, FDs, PPF) - Capital Gain (real estate, equity) - Rent (property) - NAV Appreciation (mutual funds) 2. Risk: No investment is risk-free (even government securities carry inflation risk). The fundamental principle of finance states: \[\text{Higher Expected Return} \Rightarrow \text{Higher Risk}\] 3. Liquidity: The ease with which an investment can be converted to cash without significant loss of value. Listed equity shares are highly liquid; real estate and PPF are illiquid. 4. Safety: The probability that the invested capital will be returned to the investor. Government securities score highest on safety. 5. Tax Efficiency: The ability of an investment to minimise tax liability. Instruments like ELSS, PPF, NPS, and life insurance offer tax benefits under the Income Tax Act, 1961. 6. Marketability: Whether the investment can be easily bought and sold in secondary markets. NSE and BSE provide marketability to listed securities. Comprising 15 books (adhikaranas) and 150 chapters, it covers topics ranging from treasury management to risk diversification that are strikingly relevant to modern finance. “A wise king should seek the welfare of his subjects through prosperity.” — Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I 1.5.2 Kautilya’s Wealth Principles and Modern Investment Principle 1: Artha (Wealth) is the Foundation Kautilya held that Artha — material wealth and economic prosperity — is the very foundation of Dharma (righteousness) and Kama (enjoyment). Without economic security, social and moral progress is impossible. Modern finance echoes this: financial freedom enables life choices. Modern Parallel: Emergency Fund → Financial Freedom → Life Goals Principle 2: Kosha (Treasury) — Capital Preservation First Kautilya devoted extensive attention to the Kosha (state treasury). He argued that the king must first secure existing wealth before attempting expansion. The treasury is the source of all power. Modern Parallel: Capital Preservation as the first principle in risk management — “First, do not lose money” (Warren Buffett’s Rule #1) Principle 3: Diversification of Revenue Sources Kautilya prescribed that the state derive revenues from multiple sources — agriculture, trade, mines, forests, and taxes — so that no single source failure would endanger the treasury. Modern Parallel: Portfolio Diversification — MPT’s core insight that combining uncorrelated assets reduces total risk Principle 4: Risk Assessment Before Action (Upaaya) Every major financial or military action was to be preceded by rigorous risk assessment. Kautilya identified four upayas (strategies): Sama (conciliation), Dana (gift/incentive), Bheda (division), and Danda (force). Each involved evaluating cost-benefit tradeoffs. Modern Parallel: Risk-Return Analysis before every investment decision Principle 5: Information Advantage (Intelligence) Kautilya placed extraordinary emphasis on intelligence gathering as the foundation of sound decision-making. The king was never to act on incomplete information. Modern Parallel: Fundamental Analysis, Due Diligence, Research — SEBI mandates disclosure requirements to ensure informed investment Principle 6: Long-Term Thinking (Yugas) Kautilya described governance and wealth management in terms of long cycles (yugas), emphasising that short-term sacrifices yield long-term prosperity. Modern Parallel: Long-term equity investment, Rupee Cost Averaging through SIPs, Compounding over decades 1.5.3 Comparative Table: Arthashastra vs. Modern Portfolio Management Arthashastra Principle Modern Equivalent Relevance in India Today Kosha Raksha (Treasury Protection) Capital Preservation / Risk Management SEBI’s IEPF, investor protection norms Bahubali Niti (Diversification of Power) Portfolio Diversification (MPT) Markowitz Efficient Frontier Vyavaharika Dharma (Ethical Trade) ESG Investing / Corporate Governance BRSR reporting, SEBI ESG framework Upaaya (Strategic Risk Assessment) Risk-Return Analysis / Scenario Planning VaR, Stress Testing, Scenario Analysis Danda (Enforcement / Stop-Loss) Stop-Loss Orders / Risk Limits F&O position limits, circuit breakers Kshetra Vibhaga (Resource Allocation) Asset Allocation Strategy Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) Niti (Intelligence and Research) Fundamental & Technical Analysis SEBI research analyst regulations Yugas (Long-term Cycles) Long-term Investing / Compound Interest SIP discipline, long-term wealth creation Vyaya (Controlled Expenditure) Expense Ratio Minimisation / Cost Control Direct Mutual Fund plans, zero-commission Labha (Profit Maximisation with limits) Sharpe Ratio / Risk-Adjusted Returns Risk-adjusted performance benchmarking Arthashastra Principles vs. Modern Portfolio Management Source: Compiled by the author from Kautilya (300 BCE), Sharpe et al. (2020), and SEBI publications. The key takeaways are: Investment is a sacrifice of present certainty for future uncertain return — distinguished from speculation by its research-based, long-term orientation. Three characteristics drive every investment decision: Return, Risk, and Liquidity — and these three are in perpetual tension. Classification of investments into financial (equity, debt, derivatives), physical (real estate, gold), and hybrid (REITs, SGBs) helps match instruments to investor objectives. Four primary needs drive investment: wealth creation (compounding), inflation protection (real returns), retirement planning (EPF, PPF, NPS), and tax planning (Section 80C). Indian investment avenues span a wide spectrum — from ultra-safe G-Secs and PPF to market-linked equity and real estate — each with distinct risk, return, and tax profiles. Gold and silver occupy unique positions as alternative assets — gold as inflation hedge, silver as both precious metal and industrial commodity. Kautilya’s Arthashastra reveals that the principles of modern portfolio management — capital preservation, diversification, risk assessment, long-term thinking — have deep roots in Indian intellectual tradition. 1.7 Key Terms Investment — Commitment of funds today for uncertain future returns Speculation — Short-term, high-risk financial activity based on market movements Return — Income from investment (dividend, interest, capital gain) Risk — Probability that actual return will differ from expected return Liquidity — Ease of conversion of an asset to cash Safety — Protection of invested capital Government Securities (G-Secs) — Sovereign debt instruments issued by RBI Treasury Bills — Short-term government securities (up to 364 days) Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) — RBI-issued gold-backed investment bonds PPF (Public Provident Fund) — 15-year government-backed savings scheme EPF (Employees’ Provident Fund) — Mandatory retirement scheme for salaried employees SCSS (Senior Citizens Savings Scheme) — Post office scheme for 60+ investors SSY (Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana) — Savings scheme for girl child education and marriage ULIP (Unit Linked Insurance Plan) — Market-linked insurance product by IRDAI REIT (Real Estate Investment Trust) — Listed trust owning income-generating real estate InvIT (Infrastructure Investment Trust) — Listed trust owning infrastructure assets Fixed Deposit (FD) — Bank deposit at fixed rate for fixed tenure Tax Efficiency — Minimisation of tax liability through investment planning Inflation Risk — Risk of purchasing power erosion Capital Gain — Profit from sale of investment above purchase price EEE Status — Exempt-Exempt-Exempt (contribution, accumulation, withdrawal) Section 80C — Income tax deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh for specific investments Arthashastra — Ancient Indian treatise on statecraft and economics by Kautilya Kosha — Treasury in Kautilya’s framework; Chapter 2 Financial Investments Learning Objectives After completing this unit, students will be able to: Explain the meaning, features, and types of shares, debentures, and other financial securities Distinguish between equity and preference shares, and among the types of each Analyse the structure, advantages, and risks of mutual fund investments Calculate Net Asset Value (NAV) and Expense Ratio with numerical illustrations Describe the SEBI categorisation of mutual fund schemes (2017–present) Evaluate Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs), REITs, and InvITs as investment instruments Assess the growth and future prospects of ETFs, REITs, and InvITs in the Indian market 2.1 Shares — Meaning and Features 2.1.1 What is a Share? A share is a unit of ownership in a company. When a company raises capital by issuing shares to the public, it distributes ownership of the company into small, equal units. Each unit is a share. The holder of a share is called a shareholder or stockholder and has a proportionate claim on the company’s assets and earnings. In India, shares are issued under the Companies Act, 2013 and are regulated by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India). They are traded on stock exchanges — primarily the NSE (National Stock Exchange) and BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange). “A share is not just a piece of paper — it is a proportionate ownership of a living, breathing business enterprise.” — Benjamin Graham Share Capital Structure: \[	ext{Total Equity} = 	ext{Paid-up Capital} + 	ext{Reserves and Surplus}\] \[	ext{Book Value per Share} =  rac{	ext{Total Equity}}{	ext{Number of Outstanding Shares}}\] 2.1.2 Rights of Shareholders Shareholders enjoy several fundamental rights: Right to dividend — proportionate share in distributed profits Right to vote — one share, one vote (equity shareholders) on company matters Right to information — access to annual reports, quarterly results Right to transfer — free transfer of listed shares on stock exchanges Pre-emptive right (Right Issue) — first right to subscribe to new share issues Right to residual claims — claim on assets during liquidation (after creditors) Right to attend AGM — participate in Annual General Meetings 2.2 Equity Shares 2.2.1 Meaning and Features Equity shares (also called ordinary shares or common stock) represent the primary and permanent capital of a company. Equity shareholders are the true owners of the business and bear the highest risk. Key Features: - Variable dividend — declared by the Board, not fixed - Last in dividend priority — preference shareholders paid first - Residual claimants — in liquidation, equity holders receive what remains after all liabilities - Voting rights — full voting rights in all company matters - Unlimited upside — shares of companies like Infosys, TCS, and Reliance have created immense wealth - Perpetual existence — equity capital is permanent (no redemption) 2.2.2 Types of Equity Shares Table 2.1: Table 2.2: Table 2.1: Types of Equity Shares and Indian Examples Type Features Indian Example Ordinary / Common Shares Standard equity with full voting rights and dividend entitlement Reliance Industries, TCS, HDFC Bank Founder Shares / Promoter Shares Held by founders; may carry differential voting rights (DVR) Infosys founder shares (N.R. Narayana Murthy, Nilekani) Sweat Equity Shares Issued to directors/employees for know-how or IPR at discount ESOP-heavy tech startups: Zomato, Nykaa Employee Stock Option Plan (ESOP) Options to buy shares at predetermined price; reward tool Wipro, Infosys ESOP programmes Bonus Shares Issued free to existing shareholders from reserves TCS 1:1 bonus (2022), Asian Paints frequent bonuses Right Shares Offered to existing shareholders at discount before public issue Tata Motors Rights Issue (2021 — ₹15,000 Cr) Deferred Shares Dividend deferred until preference and equity holders are paid Historically used; rare in modern India Source: Compiled from Companies Act 2013, SEBI Regulations, and NSE/BSE corporate action data. Differential Voting Rights (DVR) Shares: SEBI amended regulations in 2019 to allow superior voting right shares (SR Shares) for promoters of technology companies during their IPO. This was triggered by concerns that founders of new-age companies (like Zomato, Paytm) would lose control post-IPO to institutional investors. The concept borrows from Google’s Class A / Class B share structure. 2.3 Preference Shares 2.3.1 Meaning and Features Preference shares occupy a middle position between equity shares and debentures. Preference shareholders have a preferential right over equity shareholders in: - Payment of dividends (fixed rate) - Repayment of capital in case of winding up However, preference shareholders generally do not have voting rights (unless dividends are in arrear for two consecutive years). \[	ext{Preference Dividend} = 	ext{Face Value} 	imes 	ext{Dividend Rate (\%)}\] 2.3.2 Types of Preference Shares Table 2.3: Table 2.4: Table 2.2: Types of Preference Shares Type Description Key_Feature Cumulative Unpaid dividends accumulate; must be paid before equity dividend Investor-protective; safe during loss years Non-Cumulative Lapsed dividends are not carried forward No backlog; company-friendly Participating Right to share in surplus profits after fixed dividend Upside participation in good years Non-Participating Only entitled to fixed dividend, no additional profit share Fixed income only Redeemable Redeemed by company after a specified period (max 20 yrs in India) Capital returned; SEBI regulated Irredeemable Not redeemed during company’s lifetime (banned in India post-1988) Permanent capital; phased out Convertible Can be converted into equity shares after specified period Equity upside with preference security Non-Convertible Cannot be converted into equity Pure fixed-income; no equity participation Source: Compiled from Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI Regulations. 2.4 Debentures 2.4.1 Meaning A debenture is a debt instrument issued by a company acknowledging its indebtedness. It represents a long-term loan to the company. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, and have a legal right to receive: - Periodic interest (called coupon) - Repayment of principal at maturity In India, debentures issued to public must be listed on stock exchanges (NSE or BSE debt segment) and rated by credit rating agencies like CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, or India Ratings. 2.4.2 Types of Debentures Table 2.5: Table 2.6: Table 2.3: Types of Debentures Classification Basis Type Description On Security Secured Debentures Backed by charge on company’s assets; safer for investors Unsecured Debentures No asset backing; higher risk, higher yield On Convertibility Fully Convertible Debentures (FCDs) Entire amount converted to equity on specified date Partly Convertible Debentures (PCDs) Partial conversion to equity; balance redeemed Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) Not convertible; pure debt instrument; most common in India On Redemption Redeemable / Irredeemable Redeemable at par/premium on maturity; irredeemable rare On Coupon Fixed / Floating Rate Fixed coupon vs. linked to MIBOR/T-Bill rate Source: Compiled from Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. Bajaj Finance, HDFC, Shriram Transport Finance, and Tata Capital have issued retail NCDs with coupon rates ranging from 7.5% to 10% p.a., offering returns superior to bank FDs with credit risk. 2.5 Mutual Funds 2.5.1 Meaning and Structure A mutual fund is a professionally managed collective investment vehicle that pools money from many investors and invests in a diversified portfolio of securities. In India, mutual funds are regulated by SEBI under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 (amended multiple times through 2023). It represents the price at which investors can buy (subscription) or sell (redemption) units of the fund. \[ oxed{NAV =  rac{	ext{Total Assets} - 	ext{Total Liabilities}}{	ext{Number of Units Outstanding}}}\] Components: - Total Assets = Market value of securities + Cash and equivalents + Receivables + Accrued income - Total Liabilities = Payables + Accrued expenses + Management fee payable 2.6.2 NAV Calculation — Worked Example Example 2.1: Calculate the NAV of “Axis Bluechip Fund” given the following data as on March 31, 2024: Component Amount (₹ Crore) Equity portfolio market value 8,450 Liquid funds / Cash 320 Dividend receivable 48 Other receivables 22 Management fee payable 15 Other liabilities 8 Number of units 250 crore Solution: \[	ext{Total Assets} = 8,450 + 320 + 48 + 22 = ₹8,840 	ext{ Cr}\] \[	ext{Total Liabilities} = 15 + 8 = ₹23 	ext{ Cr}\] \[	ext{Net Assets} = 8,840 - 23 = ₹8,817 	ext{ Cr}\] \[NAV =  rac{8,817 	ext{ Cr}}{250 	ext{ Cr units}} = ₹35.27 	ext{ per unit}\] # NAV Calculation total_assets <- 8450 + 320 + 48 + 22 # in Crore total_liabilities <- 15 + 8 net_assets <- total_assets - total_liabilities units_outstanding <- 250 # Crore units NAV <- net_assets / units_outstanding cat("Total Assets: ₹", total_assets, "Crore
") ## Total Assets: ₹ 8840 Crore cat("Total Liabilities: ₹", total_liabilities, "Crore
") ## Total Liabilities: ₹ 23 Crore cat("Net Assets: ₹", net_assets, "Crore

") ## NAV per unit: ₹ 35.27 2.6.3 NAV and Returns Absolute Return: \[	ext{Absolute Return (\%)} =  rac{NAV_{current} - NAV_{purchase}}{NAV_{purchase}} 	imes 100\] CAGR (for periods > 1 year): \[CAGR = \left( rac{NAV_{current}}{NAV_{purchase}}ight)^{ rac{1}{n}} - 1\] Example 2.2: An investor purchased units of HDFC Flexi Cap Fund at NAV ₹18.50 on April 1, 2016. The NAV on March 31, 2024 was ₹52.80. Calculate absolute return and CAGR. nav_purchase <- 18.50 nav_current <- 52.80 years_held <- 8 absolute_return <- ((nav_current - nav_purchase) / nav_purchase) * 100 cagr <- (nav_current / nav_purchase)^(1/years_held) - 1 cat("Absolute Return:", round(absolute_return, 2), "%

") ## CAGR: 14.01 % per annum 2.7 Expense Ratio 2.7.1 Meaning and Importance The Expense Ratio (ER) is the annual cost charged by a mutual fund to manage an investor’s money, expressed as a percentage of the fund’s daily average AUM. It covers: - Fund management fee (largest component) - Trustee fee - Registrar and transfer agent fee - Marketing and distribution expenses (only in Regular Plans) - Audit, legal, and custodian fees \[ oxed{	ext{Expense Ratio (\%)} =  rac{	ext{Total Annual Fund Expenses}}{	ext{Average Daily AUM}} 	imes 100}\] SEBI Expense Ratio Limits (as of 2024): Table 2.7: Table 2.8: Table 2.4: SEBI Maximum TER Limits for Mutual Funds AUM Slab Equity TER Max Debt TER Max Index/ETF Max First ₹500 Cr 2.25% 2.00% 1.00% Next ₹250 Cr 2.00% 1.75% 1.00% Next ₹1,250 Cr 1.75% 1.50% 1.00% Next ₹3,000 Cr 1.60% 1.35% 1.00% Next ₹5,000 Cr 1.50% 1.25% 1.00% Next ₹40,000 Cr Reduce by 0.05% per ₹5,000 Cr Reduce by 0.05% 1.00% Balance above ₹50,000 Cr 1.05% 0.80% 1.00% Source: Compiled from RBI, SEBI, NSE, BSE, AMFI and Government Reports (Latest Available Data). 2.7.2 Expense Ratio Calculation — Worked Example Example 2.3: A mutual fund has daily average AUM of ₹12,000 Crore. This brought standardisation and comparability to India’s mutual fund landscape. ETFs combine the diversification benefits of mutual funds with the trading flexibility of stocks. Key Features of ETFs: - Passively managed (track an index) - Lower expense ratio than actively managed funds (0.05%–0.50%) - Real-time pricing (unlike NAV-based mutual funds) - Can be bought/sold anytime during market hours - Minimum investment = 1 unit (at market price) - No exit load in most cases - Require demat account (unlike regular mutual funds) ETF vs. Index Fund: Feature ETF Index Fund Trading Real-time on exchange End-of-day NAV Demat Required Not required Minimum Amount 1 unit ₹100–₹500 SIP Expense Ratio 0.05%–0.25% 0.15%–0.50% Tracking Error Slightly higher Lower Liquidity Higher (intraday) T+3 redemption ETF Growth in India: Figure 2.7: Figure 2.7: ETF AUM Growth in India (2016–2026) Source: Compiled from RBI, SEBI, NSE, BSE, AMFI and Government Reports (Latest Available Data). REITs allow retail investors to invest in large commercial properties (office parks, malls, hospitals) with a minimum of ₹10,000–15,000. The objective is to identify undervalued or overvalued securities in the market. Top-Down Approach: Fundamental analysis proceeds through four stages, in order: Economic Analysis — assess macroeconomic conditions (GDP, inflation, interest rates) Industry Analysis — assess sector attractiveness (Porter’s Five Forces, life cycle stage) Company Analysis — assess business model, moat, and governance Financial Analysis — assess valuation ratios (EPS, P/E, ROE, etc.) The output of this process is a comparison of Intrinsic Value (IV) against the current Market Price: If IV > Market Price → BUY If IV < Market Price → SELL / AVOID If IV ≈ Market Price → HOLD Figure 3.2: Top-Down Fundamental Analysis Framework 3.3 3.3 Economic Analysis 3.3.1 3.3.1 Key Macroeconomic Indicators for Indian Investors A. The five forces that determine competitive rivalry and industry profitability are: Bargaining Power of Suppliers — affects input costs Bargaining Power of Buyers — affects revenue pressure Threat of New Entrants — affects market share dilution Threat of Substitutes — affects demand shift Competitive Rivalry — the net result of the above four forces; high rivalry compresses returns Figure 3.4: Porter’s Five Forces Model Application to Indian IT Industry (TCS / Infosys): Force Assessment Impact Competitive Rivalry High (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, Accenture) Moderate — large contracts mitigate Supplier Power Low (large talent pool, though wage inflation rising) Positive Buyer Power Moderate (large MNCs have leverage; but switching costs exist) Moderate New Entrants Low (high capital + talent barriers) Positive Substitutes Rising (AI/automation threatens repetitive IT work) Negative long-term Overall: Attractive industry with strong entry barriers 3.4.2 3.4.2 Industry Life Cycle Every industry passes through four stages: Stage Characteristics Investment Strategy Introduction High losses, heavy R&D, few players High risk; potential for multi-bagger Growth Rapid revenue growth, improving margins, rising competition Best time to invest Maturity Stable growth, established players, dividend payers Value + income strategy Decline Revenue falling, exit of players, margin compression Avoid or exit Indian Industry Examples by Stage (2024): Stage Industry Examples Introduction Green Hydrogen, Space Tech NTPC Green Hydrogen, ISRO spinoffs Growth Electric Vehicles, Data Centres Tata Motors EV, Adani Data Centres Maturity FMCG, Private Banking HUL, Nestle India, HDFC Bank Decline Legacy Telecom (Wireline), Print Media Declining sector Source: Compiled from RBI, SEBI, NSE, BSE, AMFI and Government Reports (Latest Available Data). 3.5 3.5 Company Analysis 3.5.1 3.5.1 Business Model Analysis A company’s business model defines how it creates, delivers, and captures value. Key elements: Revenue Model — How does the company earn? (SaaS subscription, toll, retail, B2B) Cost Structure — Fixed vs. variable costs; operating leverage Value Proposition — Why do customers choose this company? Competitive Moat — Warren Buffett’s concept of sustainable competitive advantage Moat Analysis — Indian Companies: Company Type of Moat Evidence Asian Paints Brand + Distribution network 55,000+ dealer network; 60% market share HDFC Bank Low-cost deposit franchise + technology CASA ratio 40%+; GNPA < 1.5% TCS Scale + intellectual capital + client stickiness 95%+ client retention; $29B revenue Avenue Supermarts (D-Mart) EDLC (Every Day Low Cost) model Owned stores → no rental risk Bajaj Finance Risk analytics + cross-sell platform 85M+ customers; 30%+ ROE 3.5.2 3.5.2 Corporate Governance Assessment SEBI’s LODR (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 mandate governance standards for listed Indian companies. Investors should assess: Board composition — Independent directors ≥ 1/3 of board Audit committee — Majority independent directors Related party transactions — Scrutinise for tunnelling Promoter pledging — High pledging = governance red flag Remuneration — CEO pay vs. performance alignment Red Flag: Promoter Pledge Ratio When promoters pledge their shares to borrow money, stock price declines can trigger margin calls, forcing sell-off. A portfolio is a collection of financial investments — stocks, bonds, mutual fund units, ETFs, real estate, gold — held by an individual or institutional investor. The fundamental insight of portfolio theory is that: “The whole is different from — and often better than — the sum of its parts.” Combining assets that respond differently to market events can reduce total risk without proportionally reducing expected return. This is the mathematical basis of diversification. Portfolio vs. Individual Security: Aspect Individual Security Portfolio Risk Full company/sector risk Risk is averaged and reduced Return Dependent on single security Weighted average of all holdings Volatility Higher Lower (due to diversification) Suitability Experts / Speculators All investors Monitoring Single security Multiple holdings 5.1.2 5.1.2 Portfolio in the Indian Context Indian investors increasingly hold portfolios through: - The Markowitz model — also called Mean-Variance Analysis — provided the first rigorous mathematical framework for portfolio construction. Core Proposition: > An investor should choose portfolios that offer the maximum expected return for a given level of risk, or equivalently, the minimum risk for a given expected return. These optimal portfolios form the Efficient Frontier. 5.3.2 5.3.2 Assumptions of the Markowitz Model Investors are rational and risk-averse Decision-making is based on expected return (mean) and risk (variance/SD) Investors prefer higher return for the same risk and lower risk for the same return Returns follow a normal distribution Markets are perfectly efficient and liquid There are no taxes or transaction costs (simplified assumption) Single-period investment horizon 5.3.3 5.3.3 The Efficient Frontier The Efficient Frontier is the set of all portfolios that offer: - Maximum return for a given level of risk, OR - Minimum risk for a given level of return Portfolios below the Efficient Frontier are inefficient (dominated portfolios). Sharpe (1966), measures the excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). It answers: “How much return am I earning for every percentage point of risk I’m taking?” \[ oxed{Sharpe\ Ratio =  rac{E(R_p) - R_f}{\sigma_p}}\] Where: - \(E(R_p)\) = Portfolio return (annualised) - \(R_f\) = Risk-free rate (91-day T-bill ≈ 6.8% in India, 2024) - \(\sigma_p\) = Standard deviation of portfolio returns Interpretation: - Higher Sharpe Ratio = Better risk-adjusted performance - Sharpe > 1: Good - Sharpe > 2: Excellent - Sharpe < 0: Portfolio underperformed risk-free asset 5.7.2 5.7.2 Sharpe Ratio — Worked Example Example 5.3: Evaluate three mutual funds using Sharpe Ratio. \(R_f\) = 6.5%. funds <- c("Mirae Asset Large Cap", "HDFC Mid-Cap Opp.", "Axis Bluechip") port_returns <- c(14.2, 18.5, 12.8) # Annual returns (%) port_sds <- c(15.2, 21.8, 14.1) # Annual Std Dev (%) rf <- 6.5 # Risk-free rate (%) sharpe_ratios <- (port_returns - rf) / port_sds sharpe_df <- data.frame( Fund = funds, Return = paste0(port_returns, "%"), Std_Dev = paste0(port_sds, "%"), Excess_Return = paste0(round(port_returns - rf, 1), "%"), Sharpe_Ratio = round(sharpe_ratios, 3), Rank = rank(-sharpe_ratios) ) kable(sharpe_df, caption = "Table 5.3: Sharpe Ratio Comparison — Indian Mutual Funds", col.names = c("Fund", "Return", "Std Dev", "Excess Return", "Sharpe Ratio", "Rank"), booktabs = TRUE) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = TRUE) %>% row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#2c3e50") %>% row_spec(which.max(sharpe_ratios), bold = TRUE, background = "#eafaf1") Table 5.5: Table 5.6: Table 5.3: Sharpe Ratio Comparison — Indian Mutual Funds Fund Return Std Dev Excess Return Sharpe Ratio Rank Mirae Asset Large Cap 14.2% 15.2% 7.7% 0.507 2 HDFC Mid-Cap Opp. 18.5% 21.8% 12% 0.550 1 Axis Bluechip 12.8% 14.1% 6.3% 0.447 3 Source: Compiled from AMFI and fund house fact sheets (illustrative data for pedagogical purposes). Unlike the Sharpe Ratio, it uses beta (not standard deviation) as the risk measure, making it appropriate for well-diversified portfolios where unsystematic risk has been eliminated. \[ oxed{Treynor\ Ratio =  rac{E(R_p) - R_f}{ eta_p}}\] Comparison: Sharpe vs. Treynor Feature Sharpe Ratio Treynor Ratio Risk Measure Total risk (σ) Systematic risk (β) Best For All portfolios Well-diversified portfolios What it measures Return per unit total risk Return per unit market risk Denominator Standard deviation Beta Developed By William Sharpe (1966) Jack Treynor (1965) 5.8.2 5.8.2 Treynor Ratio — Worked Example Example 5.4: Calculate Treynor Ratio for three equity mutual funds: funds_t <- c("SBI Bluechip", "Nippon India Small Cap", "ICICI Pru Balanced Adv.") returns_t <- c(13.5, 22.0, 11.0) betas <- c(0.92, 1.28, 0.65) rf_t <- 6.5 treynor_ratios <- (returns_t - rf_t) / betas treynor_df <- data.frame( Fund = funds_t, Return = paste0(returns_t, "%"), Beta = betas, Excess_Return = paste0(round(returns_t - rf_t, 1), "%"), Treynor = round(treynor_ratios, 3), Rank = rank(-treynor_ratios) ) kable(treynor_df, caption = "Table 5.4: Treynor Ratio Comparison", col.names = c("Fund", "Return", "Beta (β)", "Excess Return", "Treynor Ratio", "Rank"), booktabs = TRUE) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover"), full_width = TRUE) %>% row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#2c3e50") Table 5.7: Table 5.8: Table 5.4: Treynor Ratio Comparison Fund Return Beta (β) Excess Return Treynor Ratio Rank SBI Bluechip 13.5% 0.92 7% 7.609 2 Nippon India Small Cap 22% 1.28 15.5% 12.109 1 ICICI Pru Balanced Adv. 11% 0.65 4.5% 6.923 3 cat("

Nippon Small Cap has high returns but also high beta — its risk-adjusted performance (Treynor) is lower. 5.9 5.9 Jensen’s Alpha 5.9.1 5.9.1 Formula and Meaning Jensen’s Alpha (Michael Jensen, 1968) measures the abnormal return generated by a portfolio above (or below) what would be expected given its level of systematic risk, as predicted by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). \[ oxed{\alpha_p = R_p - \left[R_f +  eta_p (R_m - R_f)ight]}\] Where: - \(R_p\) = Actual portfolio return - \(R_f +  eta_p(R_m - R_f)\) = CAPM-expected return (required return) - \(\alpha_p\) = Jensen’s Alpha (excess return over CAPM benchmark) Interpretation: - α > 0: Portfolio outperformed CAPM expectation — manager added value (skill) - α = 0: Portfolio performed exactly as expected for its risk level - α < 0: Portfolio underperformed CAPM — manager destroyed value 5.9.2 5.9.2 Jensen’s Alpha — Worked Example Example 5.5: Evaluate Indian mutual fund managers using Jensen’s Alpha. \(R_f\) = 6.5%, Market Return (\(R_m\)) = 13.5% (Nifty 50 TRI CAGR, 5-year) funds_j <- c("HDFC Flexi Cap", "Kotak Standard Multicap", "Parag Parikh Flexi Cap", "Nifty 50 Index Fund") actual_returns <- c(16.8, 14.2, 19.5, 13.5) # Actual returns (%) betas_j <- c(1.05, 0.98, 0.85, 1.00) # Fund betas rf_j <- 6.5 rm_j <- 13.5 # CAPM expected returns capm_returns <- rf_j + betas_j * (rm_j - Managed by PPFAS Asset Management Ltd., it features: Global diversification: 35% allocation in international equities (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft) — unique among Indian diversified equity funds Value investing philosophy: Refuses to invest in companies with governance concerns (avoided Adani group during 2023 controversy) Low portfolio turnover: Contrarian; holds stocks for 5–10 years Consistent alpha: 5-year CAGR of ~19.5% vs. Nifty 50 TRI ~13.5% — alpha of ~6% despite lower beta (0.82) Sharpe Ratio (5-year): ~0.75 (vs. Nifty ~0.50) Jensen’s Alpha (5-year): ~+5.8% Lesson for Portfolio Theory: - Even in a market as competitive as India, disciplined fund managers with strong valuation and governance principles can generate consistent alpha - Low beta (0.82) + high alpha = Superior risk-adjusted performance - PPFCF validates Markowitz’s insight: Diversification (global + domestic) reduces risk while maintaining return Research Corner 5.1: Factor Investing and Smart Beta in India Beyond the classical Markowitz framework, academic research has identified specific factors that systematically earn premium returns: Value Factor — Low P/E, P/B stocks outperform (Fama & French, 1992) Size Factor — Small-cap stocks outperform large-cap (Fama & French, 1993) Momentum Factor — Stocks with recent strong performance continue to outperform (Jegadeesh & Titman, 1993) Quality Factor — High ROE, low debt, stable earnings stocks outperform Low Volatility Factor — Low-volatility stocks outperform risk-adjusted (Baker et al., 2011) Indian Evidence: SEBI’s introduction of Smart Beta ETFs in India (2019 onwards) allows retail investors to access factor-based investing: - Nifty 50 Value 20 Index ETF (Nippon India) - Nifty 100 Low Volatility 30 ETF (DSP) - Nifty Alpha 50 ETF (Kotak) - Nifty Quality Low-Volatility 30 ETF (ICICI Prudential) Research Gap: The persistence of factor premia in Indian mid-cap and small-cap segments — especially during market stress periods (COVID-19, 2008 GFC) — is an active research area with PhD potential. Key Reference: Sehgal, S. & Balakrishnan, I. (2002). Contrarian and momentum strategies in the Indian capital market. Vikalpa, 27(1), 13–19. 5.10 5.10 Summary A portfolio is a collection of assets. Portfolio return = weighted average of individual returns. Portfolio risk ≠ weighted average risk — correlation between assets determines diversification benefit. Two-asset portfolio risk is calculated using the formula incorporating weights, standard deviations, and correlation coefficient. The lower the correlation, the greater the risk reduction. Markowitz Modern Portfolio Theory (1952) formalises the concept of the Efficient Frontier — the set of portfolios offering maximum return for each risk level. Rational investors should only hold efficient portfolios. Portfolio selection is determined by the intersection of the Efficient Frontier with the investor’s indifference curve (risk preference). Different investors choose different portfolios on the same frontier. Portfolio revision is necessary due to changing life stages, market conditions, rebalancing needs, and new opportunities. Constraints include transaction costs, taxes, lock-in restrictions, and behavioural biases. Sharpe Ratio = Excess return / Total risk (σ). Appropriate for all portfolios. Higher is better. Treynor Ratio = Excess return / Systematic risk (β). Appropriate for well-diversified portfolios. Higher is better. Jensen’s Alpha = Actual return − CAPM-expected return. Positive alpha = manager skill; negative alpha = underperformance. The most rigorous measure of investment manager performance. All three measures should be used together — they measure different dimensions of performance. A fund ranked #1 on Sharpe may not be #1 on Treynor, depending on its diversification level. 5.11 Key Terms Portfolio — Combination of financial assets held by an investor Diversification — Combining uncorrelated assets to reduce total risk Portfolio Return — Weighted average of individual asset returns Portfolio Variance — Measure of portfolio risk; depends on weights, individual risks, and correlations Covariance — Measure of how two securities move together Correlation Coefficient (ρ) — Standardised covariance; ranges from −1 to +1 Efficient Frontier — Set of optimal portfolios offering max return per risk level Minimum Variance Portfolio (MVP) — Portfolio with lowest achievable risk Capital Market Line (CML) — Line from risk-free rate tangent to Efficient Frontier Markowitz Model — Mean-variance portfolio optimisation framework Indifference Curve — Curve showing all risk-return combinations equally preferred by an investor Portfolio Revision — Periodic restructuring of portfolio to meet changing objectives Rebalancing — Restoring portfolio to target asset allocation after drift Threshold Rebalancing — Rebalance only when allocation deviates beyond a set limit Sharpe Ratio — Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation) Treynor Ratio — Excess return per unit of systematic risk (beta) Jensen’s Alpha — Actual portfolio return minus CAPM-expected return CAPM — Capital Asset Pricing Model: \(E(R_i) = R_f +  eta_i(R_m - R_f)\) Abnormal Return — Return in excess of CAPM prediction; Jensen’s Alpha Risk-Adjusted Return — Return measured relative to risk taken Tracking Error — Standard deviation of portfolio return minus benchmark return Alpha — Return above benchmark; measure of manager skill Beta (β) — Sensitivity of portfolio to market movements STT — Securities Transaction Tax; cost of equity trading in India PMS — Portfolio Management Service; SEBI-regulated discretionary portfolio management (min ₹50 lakh) AIF — Alternative Investment Fund; SEBI-regulated (min ₹1 crore) Disposition Effect — Tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long Smart Beta ETF — Index ETF with factor-based weighting (value, quality, momentum) Factor Investing — Investment approach targeting specific return-generating factors Information Ratio — Jensen’s Alpha divided by tracking error; measures consistency of alpha 5.12 Review Questions — Unit V 5.12.1 Very Short Answer Questions Define portfolio in the context of investment management. Chapter 6 Trading View Practicals 6.1 Program 1: SMA Trend Identification & Dynamic Support/Resistance Objective Identify trend direction and find dynamic support/resistance levels using the Simple Moving Average (SMA) — applied here to Indian stock market (NSE/BSE) charts on TradingView. Steps Step 1: Go to TradingView and Open the Chart Section Open your browser and navigate to tradingview.com. Sign in to your account (or create one if you haven’t already — it’s free). From the top navigation bar, click on “Products” or directly click “Chart” to launch the chart workspace. Step 2: Select an NSE Stock and Set the Timeframe Click on the symbol search bar at the top-left of the chart (it may currently show a default ticker). Type the stock name — for example, RELIANCE. From the dropdown results, make sure to select the listing tagged NSE (National Stock Exchange of India), since TradingView also lists the same company on other exchanges. It should appear as NSE:RELIANCE. Other popular NSE examples you can try: NSE:TCS, NSE:HDFCBANK, NSE:INFY, NSE:ICICIBANK, NSE:SBIN. Once selected, the candlestick chart for Reliance Industries will load, denominated in ₹ (INR). Now set the timeframe for long-term investing analysis. Click on the timeframe selector in the top toolbar (it usually shows “1D” by default). Select 1W (1 Week) from the dropdown, or type 1W directly into the timeframe box and press Enter. The chart will now display weekly candles — each candle represents one full week of trading on NSE, which smooths out daily noise and is ideal for long-term trend analysis. Why weekly timeframe for Indian long-term investing? NSE has frequent intraday volatility, especially around results season, RBI policy announcements, and budget days. A weekly chart filters this noise and reveals the broader trend more reliably for long-term positioning. Step 3: Open the Indicators Panel Look at the top toolbar of the chart and click on “Indicators” (it may show as “Indicators” with an fx or function-style icon, sometimes abbreviated visually). A panel titled “Indicators & Strategies” will pop up, with a search bar at the top. In the search box, type “Simple Moving Average”. You’ll see one or more matching results in the list (TradingView sometimes shows it twice — once as a standalone built-in indicator, and once under community scripts). Use the built-in “Moving Average Simple” — it’s the official one maintained by TradingView and is sufficient for this exercise. Step 4: Add the SMA and Set the Length to 50 Click on “Moving Average Simple” from the search results. It will be added to your chart instantly with a default length (usually 9). To customize it, click the gear/settings icon next to the SMA name in the legend at the top-left of the chart (it appears once the indicator is added), or double-click directly on the SMA line on the chart. In the settings window that opens, find the “Length” field under the Inputs tab. Clear the existing value and type 50. Click OK to apply. The chart will now redraw with a 50-period SMA line overlaid on the weekly candles. Since you’re on the weekly timeframe, this represents the 50-week SMA — roughly the average closing price over the last ~50 weeks (about 11–12 months), which is a popular long-term trend filter among Indian long-term investors and positional traders. Step 5: Interpret the SMA on the Chart Once the SMA 50 is plotted, observe where the current price sits relative to the line: Price Above SMA 50 → Uptrend: The stock is trading above its 50-week average, suggesting sustained buying interest and a bullish long-term structure. Many Indian portfolio managers use this as a basic “trend filter” before considering fresh long-term buys. Price Below SMA 50 → Downtrend: The stock is trading below its 50-week average, signaling weakness or a corrective/bearish phase. This is often used as a caution flag to avoid fresh long-term entries or to review existing holdings. SMA as Dynamic Support or Resistance: Unlike a fixed horizontal support/resistance line, the SMA moves with price over time. In an uptrend, the SMA 50 frequently acts as a “floor” where price pulls back to and bounces from. In a downtrend, it often acts as a “ceiling” that price rallies up to and gets rejected from. Trading Rules Signal Condition Action  BUY Price approaches the 50 SMA from above and bounces off it (forms a reversal candle near the line) Consider entering or adding to a long-term position  SELL Price approaches the 50 SMA from below and gets rejected (fails to close above it) Consider booking profits or avoiding fresh entry Indian market context note: Apply this technique to liquid, fundamentally sound NSE large-cap or Nifty 50 stocks for long-term investing decisions. For small-cap or low-liquidity stocks, SMA bounces can be less reliable due to erratic price action and lower trading volumes. Always combine this technical signal with basic fundamental checks (sector outlook, quarterly results, promoter holding trends) before making investment decisions — this manual covers a technical tool, not complete investment advice. Practice Exercise Open NSE:TCS on the weekly timeframe and add a 50 SMA. Identify whether the stock is currently in an uptrend or downtrend based on price position relative to the SMA. Scroll back through the last 2–3 years of price history and mark at least two instances where price bounced off the 50 SMA, and one instance where it was rejected by the SMA. Repeat the exercise for NSE:HDFCBANK and compare the trend structure between the two stocks. Key Takeaways The 50 SMA on a weekly chart is a simple, widely-used trend filter for long-term investing decisions on NSE-listed stocks. Price position relative to the SMA (above vs. below) gives a quick read on the prevailing trend. The SMA also acts as a dynamic support/resistance zone, offering potential entry (bounce) and exit (rejection) cues. Always combine this with broader market context (Nifty 50 trend, sector performance) before acting on signals from a single stock chart. 6.2 Program 2: EMA Crossover Breakout Strategy Objective To identify breakout and momentum opportunities using the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) crossover technique — applied to Indian stock market (NSE/BSE) charts on TradingView. Why EMA instead of SMA here? The Exponential Moving Average (EMA) gives more weight to recent price action compared to the SMA, making it react faster to new momentum. This makes it well-suited for spotting breakouts early — useful for Indian long-term investors who want to catch the start of a fresh up-move in stocks like Nifty 50 constituents. Steps Step 1: Open the Indicators Panel With your NSE stock chart open, click on “Indicators” in the top toolbar of the chart (shown with an fx-style icon, labeled “Indicators”). The “Indicators & Strategies” search panel will open. Step 2: Search for “Moving Average Exponential” In the search bar at the top of the panel, type “Moving Average Exponential”. From the results list, select the built-in “Moving Average Exponential” indicator (maintained directly by TradingView, distinct from any community/script versions). Step 3: Add the First EMA — Set Length to 20, Color Green Once selected, the EMA will be added to your chart with a default length (usually 9). Click the gear/settings icon next to the EMA’s name in the chart legend (top-left of the chart) to open its settings. Under the Inputs tab, change the Length field to 20. Switch to the Style tab and change the line color to Green for easy visual identification. Click OK to apply. Your chart now shows a 20-period EMA in green — on the weekly timeframe, this is your 20-week EMA, representing short-to-medium-term momentum. Step 4: Duplicate the EMA to Add a Second One In the chart legend (top-left), right-click on the EMA 20 entry — or click the three-dot menu (⋮) next to it. From the dropdown menu, select “Duplicate”. This creates an exact copy of the EMA 20 indicator, stacked on the same chart, which you’ll now modify into a second, longer-period EMA. Step 5: Configure the Second EMA — Set Length to 50, Color Red Click the gear/settings icon next to the newly duplicated EMA in the legend. Under the Inputs tab, change the Length from 20 to 50. Switch to the Style tab and change the line color to Red. Click OK to apply. Your chart now displays two EMAs: EMA 20 (Green) — faster, tracks short-term momentum EMA 50 (Red) — slower, tracks the broader trend Step 6: Observe the EMA Crossovers on the Chart With both EMAs plotted, watch for the points where the green (20) line crosses the red (50) line: These crossover points are the core signal of this strategy and will appear at multiple points across the stock’s price history on NSE charts — particularly visible during strong trending phases like post-results rallies or sectoral rotations. Interpretation Crossover Type Visual Cue Meaning  20 EMA crosses above 50 EMA Green line moves above red line Bullish Breakout — short-term momentum is turning positive relative to the broader trend  20 EMA crosses below 50 EMA Green line moves below red line Bearish Breakout — short-term momentum is turning negative relative to the broader trend Indian market context note: This is sometimes informally compared to a faster version of the “Golden Cross / Death Cross” concept widely followed in Indian financial media (where 50-day/200-day crossovers are reported for the Nifty 50 and Sensex). The 20/50 EMA crossover on a weekly chart is a more sensitive, earlier-warning version suited for individual NSE stocks rather than just benchmark indices. Trading Rule  BUY: Enter when there is a bullish crossover (20 EMA crosses above 50 EMA) AND the current price is trading above both EMAs. This double confirmation — crossover plus price position — helps filter out weak or false breakout signals that can occur in choppy, sideways NSE stock action.  SELL / AVOID: Treat a bearish crossover (20 EMA crosses below 50 EMA) with price below both EMAs as a signal to avoid fresh entries or to review existing long positions in that stock. Practice Exercise Open NSE:INFY on the Weekly timeframe and apply both the 20 EMA (green) and 50 EMA (red) as described above. Scroll through the last 2–3 years of price history and identify at least two bullish crossovers and one bearish crossover. For each bullish crossover found, check whether price was trading above both EMAs at that point — this confirms whether it met the full BUY rule. Repeat with NSE:SBIN and compare how frequently crossovers occur in a banking stock versus an IT stock — note any difference in reliability or noise. Key Takeaways The EMA reacts faster to price than the SMA, making the 20/50 EMA crossover a useful tool for spotting early breakout momentum in NSE stocks. A crossover alone is not sufficient — always confirm with price position relative to both EMAs before acting, to avoid false signals in sideways markets. This strategy works best on liquid, fundamentally strong stocks and during clearly trending market phases; it can generate frequent false signals during range-bound or highly volatile periods, which are common around Indian budget announcements, RBI policy days, and global macro events. Combine EMA crossover signals with the broader trend context from Program 1 (SMA 50) for a more complete long-term investing view. 6.3 Program 3: VWAP Intraday Trend Strategy Objective To trade intraday using the Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) on Indian stock market (NSE) charts on TradingView. Important context shift: Unlike Programs 1 and 2, which used weekly charts for long-term trend analysis, this strategy is intraday — meaning all trading activity happens and is squared off within the same trading session. On NSE, the cash market trading session runs from 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM IST. If you place an intraday order (commonly labeled MIS — Margin Intraday Square-off — with most Indian brokers like Zerodha, Upstox, or Groww), it will be automatically closed out by the broker shortly before market close if you haven’t exited manually, typically around 3:15–3:20 PM IST. VWAP resets fresh at the start of every new trading day and is not meant to be analyzed across multiple days like the SMA/EMA in earlier programs. Steps Step 1: Set the Timeframe to 5 Minutes With your NSE stock chart open, click on the timeframe selector in the top toolbar (it may currently show “1D”, “1W”, or whatever was last used). Select 5m (5 Minutes) from the dropdown, or type 5 directly into the timeframe box and press Enter. The chart will now display 5-minute candles — each candle represents 5 minutes of trading activity within the NSE session. This shorter timeframe is essential for intraday strategies, as it captures the granular price-volume action needed for VWAP analysis. Step 2: Open the Indicators Panel Click on “Indicators” in the top toolbar (shown with the fx-style icon). The “Indicators & Strategies” search panel will open with a search bar at the top. Step 3: Search and Add “VWAP” In the search box, type VWAP. From the results, select the built-in “VWAP” indicator (officially maintained by TradingView). Click on it once to add it directly to your chart — no length or period setting is required, since VWAP is a session-based (intraday-anchored) indicator by default and recalculates automatically from the start of each trading session. Step 4: VWAP Added to the Chart The VWAP line will now appear overlaid on your 5-minute candlestick chart. Notice that the VWAP line starts fresh each trading day from the 9:15 AM opening candle and builds up through the session as more price and volume data accumulates — it does not carry over from the previous day. As the day progresses, observe how price weaves above and below this line, and how the line itself smooths out compared to the choppier candle action. Interpretation Observation Visual Cue Meaning  Price Above VWAP Candles trading above the VWAP line Indicates institutional buying — large players (FIIs, DIIs, mutual funds) are likely accumulating at or above this average price, a bullish intraday signal  Price Below VWAP Candles trading below the VWAP line Indicates selling pressure — large sell orders are weighing on price below the session average, a bearish intraday signal ⚫ VWAP as Intraday Support/Resistance Price repeatedly touching and reacting to the VWAP line The VWAP line itself often behaves like a dynamic support (in an uptrending session) or resistance (in a downtrending session) level through the day Why VWAP matters in the Indian intraday context: Institutional desks, mutual funds, and FII/DII trading desks frequently use VWAP as a benchmark to evaluate whether their own large block orders on NSE are executing at favorable prices. Because of this, VWAP tends to act as a genuine “fair value” reference point during the day — retail intraday traders watch it for the same reason, making it a self-reinforcing level. Trading Rule  BUY: Enter when price pulls back to the VWAP line and reverses upward — i.e., the stock dips down to touch or approach VWAP during an otherwise uptrending session, forms a reversal candle (such as a bullish engulfing or hammer-like candle), and resumes its move higher. This suggests the pullback found support at the institutional average price level.  AVOID / EXIT: If price breaks decisively below VWAP and stays below it, treat this as a loss of intraday bullish momentum — consider exiting existing long positions rather than holding through the session. A Note on Risk Management for Indian Intraday Trading Since this is an intraday (MIS) strategy, always set a stop-loss below recent swing lows or a fixed percentage of capital risk per trade — NSE intraday volatility (especially around results, RBI announcements, or global cues like US Fed decisions) can move prices sharply within minutes. Be mindful of margin and leverage rules set by SEBI and your broker for intraday (MIS) trades — leverage amounts vary by stock and broker, and positions must be squared off within the same session or they may be auto-closed by your broker’s risk management system (RMS), sometimes at unfavorable prices. Avoid taking fresh intraday VWAP trades in the first 5–10 minutes after market open (9:15–9:25 AM), as this period often sees erratic price discovery before VWAP becomes a meaningful reference. Practice Exercise Open NSE:HDFCBANK on the 5-minute timeframe during a live trading session (9:15 AM – 3:30 PM IST) and add the VWAP indicator. Track the stock for at least one hour and note every instance where price touches the VWAP line. Identify whether each touch resulted in a bounce (continuation of trend) or a breakdown (trend reversal). Repeat this observation on a different day with NSE:TCS and compare how VWAP behaves on a relatively calmer IT stock versus a more news-sensitive banking stock. Key Takeaways VWAP is a session-based intraday indicator that resets daily and reflects the true volume-weighted average price paid by all market participants during that NSE trading session. Price position relative to VWAP gives a quick read on whether institutional money is net buying or net selling during the day. VWAP pullback-and-reversal setups offer disciplined intraday entry points, but always pair them with a stop-loss given the leveraged nature of intraday trading. This strategy is best suited to liquid, high-volume NSE large-cap stocks; thinly traded stocks can produce unreliable VWAP signals due to inconsistent volume. 6.4 Program 3B: Anchored VWAP for Long-Term Investing Objective To adapt the Volume-Weighted Average Price concept for long-term investing using Anchored VWAP (AVWAP) — a version of VWAP that does not reset daily, making it usable across weeks, months, and years on NSE stock charts. Program 3 covered the standard session VWAP, which resets every trading day and is built specifically for intraday use — it has no meaningful interpretation on weekly or monthly charts. However, the underlying idea behind VWAP (the average price weighted by how much volume traded at each price level) is genuinely useful for long-term investors too — it just needs a different version of the tool. Anchored VWAP (AVWAP) solves this. Instead of recalculating from the start of each day, you manually “anchor” it to a specific date you choose — such as a 52-week low, a major results announcement, or the start of a financial year — and it then calculates the volume-weighted average price continuously from that anchor point forward, for as long as you want to track it (weeks, months, or years). Key distinction: Session VWAP answers “did today’s buyers get a fair price today?” Anchored VWAP answers “what is the average price paid by everyone who has bought this stock since this important date?” The second question is far more relevant to long-term investing. Steps Step 1: Set the Timeframe With your NSE stock chart open, click on the timeframe selector in the top toolbar. Select 1D (Daily) for a medium-term view, or 1W (Weekly) for a more zoomed-out long-term view — both work well with Anchored VWAP since, unlike session VWAP, it doesn’t depend on the candle interval. For this exercise, use the Daily (1D) timeframe, as it gives you finer control over picking an exact anchor date in the next step. Step 2: Open the Indicators Panel Click on “Indicators” in the top toolbar (the fx-style icon). The “Indicators & Strategies” search panel will open. Step 3: Search and Add “Anchored VWAP” In the search box, type Anchored VWAP. From the results, select the built-in “Anchored VWAP” indicator (maintained directly by TradingView — distinct from any community scripts with similar names). Click on it once. TradingView will typically place the anchor automatically at the leftmost visible candle on your current chart view as a starting default. Step 4: Choose and Set Your Anchor Point This is the most important step — the anchor date you pick determines what the AVWAP line represents. Common long-term investing anchor points for Indian stocks include: 52-week low — to see the average price paid by everyone who has bought since the stock’s worst point in the last year (useful for spotting value re-accumulation). Start of the financial year (April 1st) or calendar year (January 1st) — to track average cost basis for the current investing year, aligned with how Indian mutual funds and DIIs often report performance. Day after a major quarterly results announcement — to see how the market has averaged price in reaction to that specific result. A major budget day or RBI policy announcement — to study sustained reactions to macro events affecting Indian markets. To set this: Click and drag the anchor marker directly on the chart to your chosen date, or Click the gear/settings icon next to “Anchored VWAP” in the chart legend, go to the Inputs tab, and manually enter the specific anchor date. Click OK to apply. The AVWAP line will now begin plotting from your selected anchor date and continue forward to the present day. Step 5: Anchored VWAP Added to the Chart You will now see a single VWAP line starting from your chosen anchor point and extending across all subsequent daily (or weekly) candles, smoothing as more time passes. Unlike session VWAP, this line does not reset — it keeps calculating cumulatively from the anchor date until you change or remove it. You can add multiple Anchored VWAPs with different anchor dates on the same chart (e.g., one anchored to the 52-week low and another anchored to April 1st) by repeating Steps 3–4 and assigning each a different color for clarity. Interpretation Observation Visual Cue Meaning  Price Above Anchored VWAP Candles trading above the AVWAP line The average buyer since the anchor date is in profit — reflects sustained accumulation and bullish sentiment since that event  Price Below Anchored VWAP Candles trading below the AVWAP line The average buyer since the anchor date is at a loss — reflects distribution or weak sentiment since that event ⚫ AVWAP as Long-Term Support/Resistance Price repeatedly returning to and reacting off the AVWAP line The anchored level often acts as a “memory” price — a zone where long-term holders defend their average cost, creating real support or resistance Indian market context: Anchored VWAP is particularly useful around results season (Q1–Q4 earnings on NSE) and around Union Budget day, since Indian institutional investors (FIIs/DIIs) often re-anchor their own cost-basis tracking to these dates. Watching where price sits relative to a results-day or budget-day AVWAP gives a sense of whether the broader market has digested that event positively or negatively over the following weeks and months. Trading Rule  BUY: Consider entering or adding to a long-term position when price pulls back to a meaningful Anchored VWAP (e.g., one anchored to the 52-week low or to the start of the financial year) and shows signs of holding/reversing upward — similar logic to the SMA 50 bounce rule in Program 1, but using a volume-weighted reference instead of a simple price average.  CAUTION: If price decisively breaks below a long-standing Anchored VWAP that has acted as support for multiple weeks or months, treat this as a signal that the long-term holder base may be turning net negative — review the position or fundamental thesis before adding further. Combining With Earlier Programs This chapter works well alongside the tools from Programs 1 and 2: Use SMA 50 (Program 1) for a general trend filter. Use EMA 20/50 crossover (Program 2) for momentum confirmation. Use Anchored VWAP (this chapter) anchored to a meaningful event (52-week low, financial year start, major results date) as a volume-aware reference for “fair value since that event” — adding a layer that pure moving averages don’t capture, since AVWAP factors in how much was traded at each price, not just the price itself. Practice Exercise Open NSE:TCS on the Daily timeframe and add an Anchored VWAP anchored to its most recent 52-week low. Note whether the current price is above or below this AVWAP line, and what that implies about the average long-term buyer’s position. Add a second Anchored VWAP, this time anchored to April 1st of the current financial year, in a different color. Compare the two AVWAP lines — are they close together or far apart? What does the gap between them suggest about how sentiment has shifted across the year? Repeat with NSE:ICICIBANK, anchoring to its last quarterly results date, and observe how price has behaved relative to that post-results AVWAP since. Key Takeaways Standard session VWAP (Program 3) is strictly an intraday tool and resets daily — it cannot be meaningfully used for long-term analysis. Anchored VWAP (AVWAP) solves this by letting you fix the starting point manually, making the volume-weighted average price concept usable across weeks, months, or years. Choosing the right anchor date (52-week low, financial year start, major results/budget day) is what makes AVWAP meaningful — an arbitrary anchor produces an arbitrary line. AVWAP works best as a complementary tool alongside SMA/EMA trend analysis, since it adds a volume dimension that simple moving averages do not account for. 6.5 Program 4: MACD Momentum Strategy Objective To identify trend strength and potential reversals using the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) indicator — applied to Indian stock market (NSE/BSE) charts on TradingView for long-term investing decisions. What makes MACD different from Programs 1 and 2? SMA and EMA are plotted directly on the price chart as overlays. MACD, by contrast, is an oscillator — it appears in a separate panel below the main price chart and measures the relationship between two EMAs (typically 12 and 26 period) along with a signal line and a histogram. This makes it especially useful for spotting momentum shifts and divergences that price-only overlays can miss. Steps Step 1: Go to TradingView and Open Your Stock Chart Open your browser and navigate to tradingview.com. Sign in to your account. Search for and select your NSE stock — for example, type RELIANCE in the symbol search bar and choose the listing tagged NSE (it should appear as NSE:RELIANCE). Set the timeframe to 1W (1 Week) using the timeframe selector in the top toolbar, so the chart displays weekly candles suitable for long-term analysis. Step 2: Open the Indicators Panel Click on “Indicators” in the top toolbar of the chart (shown with the fx-style icon). The “Indicators & Strategies” search panel will open. Step 3: Search and Add MACD In the search box, type MACD. From the results list, select the built-in “MACD” (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) indicator — the official one maintained by TradingView. Click on it once to add it to your chart. By default it uses the standard settings: a 12-period EMA, a 26-period EMA, and a 9-period signal line — these defaults work well for weekly NSE stock analysis and generally don’t need to be changed for this exercise. Step 4: MACD Added Below the Chart Unlike SMA/EMA, the MACD indicator does not sit on top of the price candles. Instead, it opens in a separate panel directly below your main chart. In this panel, you’ll see three components: MACD Line (typically blue) — the difference between the 12-period and 26-period EMA. Signal Line (typically orange/red) — a 9-period EMA of the MACD line itself, used to generate crossover signals. Histogram (vertical bars, usually green/red) — visually represents the gap between the MACD line and the signal line; taller bars indicate stronger momentum in that direction. You’ll also notice a horizontal zero line running through the middle of this panel — this is a key reference level used in the trading rule below. Interpretation Signal Visual Cue Meaning  MACD Line Crossing Above Signal Line Blue line crosses upward over the orange/red signal line Buy signal — momentum is turning positive  MACD Line Crossing Below Signal Line Blue line crosses downward below the orange/red signal line Sell signal — momentum is turning negative  Divergence Price makes a new high/low on the main chart, but MACD fails to make a corresponding new high/low Reversal Signal — momentum is weakening even though price is still extending, often an early warning of a trend change Understanding Divergence in the Indian context: Divergence is one of the most valuable uses of MACD for long-term NSE investors. For example, if a stock like NSE:HDFCBANK makes a new 52-week high but the MACD line makes a lower high compared to its previous peak, this is called bearish divergence — it suggests the rally is losing underlying momentum even though price looks strong, often preceding a correction. The reverse (price making a lower low while MACD makes a higher low) is bullish divergence, often seen near the end of prolonged corrections in quality stocks. Trading Rule  BUY: Enter when there is a MACD crossover above the zero line — meaning the MACD line not only crosses above the signal line, but the crossover itself occurs while the MACD line is in positive territory (above the zero line on the panel). This combination signals that momentum has turned bullish and is strong enough to be in positive territory, filtering out weaker crossover signals that happen deep in negative territory during a still-strong downtrend. Why the zero line matters: A crossover that happens below the zero line, while it can still mark a momentum shift, often happens during weak, range-bound, or recovering downtrends and tends to be less reliable for committing fresh long-term capital. Waiting for the crossover to occur above the zero line adds a layer of trend confirmation, similar in spirit to combining EMA crossovers with price position in Program 2. Combining With Earlier Programs MACD works well as a complementary momentum check alongside the trend tools from Programs 1 and 2: Use SMA 50 (Program 1) to confirm the stock is in a broad uptrend (price above the SMA). Use EMA 20/50 crossover (Program 2) to confirm short-term momentum aligns with the long-term trend. Use MACD (this chapter) as a final momentum and divergence check — particularly useful for catching early warning signs of trend exhaustion in stocks that otherwise look strong on the SMA/EMA overlays alone. Practice Exercise Open NSE:TCS on the Weekly timeframe and add the MACD indicator with default settings. Scroll through the last 2–3 years of price history and identify at least two MACD crossovers that occurred above the zero line, and one that occurred below it. Compare how price behaved after each type of crossover — did the above-zero-line crossovers tend to lead to stronger, more sustained moves? Look for any instance of bullish or bearish divergence between price and the MACD line on this chart, and note what happened to price in the weeks following that divergence. Repeat with NSE:ICICIBANK and compare the frequency and reliability of MACD signals between a banking stock and an IT stock. Key Takeaways MACD is a momentum oscillator that sits below the price chart and tracks the relationship between a fast and slow EMA, helping identify both trend strength and early signs of reversal. MACD line crossovers above/below the signal line generate basic buy/sell signals, while divergence between price and MACD often provides earlier warning of a weakening trend than price action alone. Requiring the crossover to occur above the zero line adds a useful filter, helping long-term investors avoid weaker signals that occur during shaky or recovering downtrends. MACD is most effective when used alongside trend-confirmation tools like SMA and EMA (Programs 1 and 2) rather than in isolation, especially for long-term investing decisions on NSE stocks.
